summary: Defines a pseudo-random function extension to GSS-API for keying application protocols once a GSS-API security context exists. Its main use is to key secure session layers that cannot use per-message integrity and wrap tokens. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: After two programs have proven who they are, they need fresh secret keys. This gives them a way to make those keys from what they already share.

questions: how to derive keys from a gss-api context
subtitle: A GSS-API function that turns an established security context into fresh keying material for other protocols.

tldr.problem: Applications can use the GSS-API to authenticate, but not for transport security. The API gave them no way to get keying material out of an established security context.
tldr.mechanism: GSS_Pseudo_random() applies the context's keyed pseudo-random function to caller-supplied input and returns output of the requested length. Both peers get the same result from the same inputs.
tldr.outcome: Applications can key their own cryptographic protocols from a GSS-API context without ever seeing the raw session keys.

today: RFC 4401 is a Proposed Standard from February 2006. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it has no IANA actions.

sections.title: The Need for Keying Material
sections.content:
Some applications use the GSS-API (RFC 2743) for authentication but not for transport security, for whatever reasons. Since the API offered no method for obtaining keying material from established security contexts, these applications could not make effective use of it.

This memo defines a pseudo-random function (PRF) extension to the GSS-API. It is an abstract API extension to GSS-API version 2, update 1, with C bindings. It is not a revision of GSS-API, so how portable applications detect support for it is deferred to an expected, comprehensive update.
sections.eli5: Imagine two friends who share a secret handshake and now want new secret codes for another game. This gives them a safe way to invent the codes.

sections.title: The GSS_Pseudo_random() Call
sections.content:
The function takes a context handle, a prf_key selector, an input octet string prf_in and an integer desired_output_len. It returns a major status, a minor status and the output octet string prf_out.

It applies the context mechanism's keyed PRF to prf_in, using key material tied to the security context, and returns exactly the requested number of octets.

Limits: the minimum input length is one octet and the minimum output length is one. Mechanisms MUST consume all input of 2^14 or fewer octets and MUST be able to output at least 2^14 octets. If a mechanism cannot consume the input or produce the output, it MUST return GSS_S_FAILURE.
sections.eli5: You hand the machine a phrase and say how long a code you want. It stirs in the shared secret and gives back a code of that length, and your friend's machine gives the same one.

sections.title: Choosing Which Key: prf_key
sections.content:
The prf_key value tells the mechanism which key to use. The defined values are GSS_C_PRF_KEY_FULL (0 in the C bindings), GSS_C_PRF_KEY_PARTIAL (1) and any mechanism-specific values.

GSS_C_PRF_KEY_FULL is the best key available for a fully established context. GSS_C_PRF_KEY_PARTIAL corresponds to a key that would have been used while the context was only partially established, even if it is fully established by the time of the call. For some mechanisms the two values may refer to the same key. For mechanisms like the Kerberos V mechanism (RFC 1964), where one peer may assert a key that may be considered better, they MAY differ.
sections.eli5: There may be a good key and an earlier, weaker one. You say which one you want to use for stirring.

sections.title: Required Properties
sections.content:
The function must behave like a real PRF, and the RFC lists five properties:

  • The output MUST be a pseudo-random function of the input, keyed with context key material.
  • The initiator and acceptor MUST get the same result from the same inputs, however many times it is called while the context is unexpired.
  • Once the context is fully established, all keys and negotiations used for any prf_key MUST be authenticated, mutually if mutual authentication is in effect.
  • PRF outputs and per-message tokens MUST be cryptographically separate: knowing one must not help recover keys or transform the other.
  • It MUST NOT be possible to read any raw keys of a context through the function.
sections.eli5: Both friends must get the same code, the code must look random, and nobody can work backwards to the original secret.

sections.title: Status Codes and C Bindings
sections.content:
The C binding is gss_pseudo_random(), which takes a minor status pointer, the context, an int prf_key, an input buffer, a ssize_t desired output length and an output buffer. The C bindings add two major status codes, GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_READ and GSS_S_CALL_INACCESSIBLE_WRITE, described in RFC 2744.

Beyond success, the main failures are a null or expired context, a mechanism or context that cannot supply the requested key (including a context not yet ready), and general failure such as zero-length input or output.
sections.eli5: If you ask with no connection, an old connection, or ask for nothing, the machine says no and tells you why.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms should build their PRF from a key derived from the context's authenticated session keys and preserve the forward security properties of their key exchanges. Some mechanisms support the function on contexts that are not fully established, but applications MUST assume authentication has not completed until the context is fully established.

Callers should avoid calling the function with the same inputs by accident. A useful convention is to prepend a string naming the purpose of the output to prf_in. A PRF can safely produce only limited output, and the safe amount varies by PRF, so unless you are a qualified cryptographer, limit the output used to the necessary minimum (see RFC 4086).

Large inputs or outputs can be costly for some mechanisms, which could enable denial of service. Applications SHOULD limit the size of input strings received from peers without integrity protection.
sections.eli5: Do not ask for more secret codes than you need, give each use its own label, and do not let strangers make you do huge amounts of work.

items.label: Null context
items.desc: A null context was given as input.

items.label: Expired context
items.desc: An expired context was given as input.

items.label: Unavailable
items.desc: No mechanism support, context not ready for the prf_key, or key not available.

items.label: General failure
items.desc: For example input too large or empty, or zero output length.
